questions.stem: The electrical power dissipated in a resistor of resistance R carrying current I is
questions.explanation: Starting from $P = IV$ and substituting $V = IR$ gives $P = I(IR) = I^{2}R$. This is the heating power in the resistor. $IR$ is the potential difference, not the power.

distractorRationale.a: IR is Ohm's law for potential difference, whose unit is the volt, not the watt
distractorRationale.c: I/R has no useful interpretation here and does not have the unit of power
distractorRationale.d: This is the reciprocal of I²R and would have the unit 1/watt

questions.stem: One kilowatt-hour is equal to
questions.explanation: A kilowatt-hour is 1 kW running for 1 hour: $1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$. This is the unit on a Nigerian electricity bill. Dividing or multiplying by an extra factor of 100 or 1000 produces the distractors.

distractorRationale.a: This is 1 kW × 3.6 s, or 1000 × 3.6, missing the conversion of one hour into 3600 seconds
distractorRationale.b: This is 1000 × 360, as if an hour had 360 seconds
distractorRationale.d: This is 1000 W × 3600 s × 100, an extra factor of 100

questions.stem: An electric iron is marked 1000 W, 250 V. The current it draws from a 250 V supply is
questions.explanation: From $P = IV$, the current is $I = P/V = 1000/250 = 4.0\ \text{A}$. That is a typical current for a pressing iron on the 220–250 V PHCN supply, which is why it needs a thick cable and a well-fused socket.

distractorRationale.a: This is V/P = 250/1000, inverting the formula
distractorRationale.c: This quotes the voltage as if it were the current
distractorRationale.d: This is P × V = 1000 × 250, multiplying instead of dividing

questions.stem: A heating coil of resistance 24 Ω is connected to a 12 V supply. Calculate the power dissipated in the coil. Give your answer in watts.
questions.explanation: The convenient form is $P = \frac{V^{2}}{R} = \frac{12^{2}}{24} = \frac{144}{24} = 6.0\ \text{W}$. The same result follows from $I = V/R = 12/24 = 0.50\ \text{A}$ and $P = IV = 12 \times 0.50 = 6.0\ \text{W}$, or $P = I^{2}R = (0.50)^{2} \times 24 = 6.0\ \text{W}$.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp is left on for 2.0 hours. The electrical energy it converts is
questions.explanation: Energy $W = Pt$. Convert 2.0 hours to seconds: $t = 2.0 \times 3600 = 7200\ \text{s}$. Then $W = 60 \times 7200 = 4.32 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$. Equivalently, $0.060\ \text{kW} \times 2.0\ \text{h} = 0.12\ \text{kWh} = 0.12 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 4.32 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$.

distractorRationale.a: This is 60 × 2, leaving the time in hours instead of converting to seconds
distractorRationale.c: This is 60 × 120, treating 2 hours as 120 seconds (or as 2 minutes)
distractorRationale.d: This is 60 × 3600, the energy for 1 hour rather than 2 hours

questions.stem: A 2.0 kW heater is used for 5.0 hours. If electricity is charged at ₦40 per kWh, calculate the cost of using the heater. Give your answer in naira.
questions.explanation: Energy consumed $= 2.0\ \text{kW} \times 5.0\ \text{h} = 10\ \text{kWh}$. Cost $= 10 \times 40 = \text{₦}400$. Working in watts and seconds first is possible but slower: $W = 2000 \times 18000 = 3.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J} = 10\ \text{kWh}$, then multiply by the tariff.

questions.stem: An electric iron marked 1000 W, 240 V is used for 3.0 hours a day for 5 days. If the tariff is ₦50 per kWh, the cost of the energy consumed is
questions.explanation: Power in kilowatts is $1000\ \text{W} = 1.0\ \text{kW}$. Energy $= 1.0 \times 3.0 \times 5 = 15\ \text{kWh}$. Cost $= 15 \times 50 = \text{₦}750$. The 240 V rating is not needed for the bill; it would be used only if you were asked for the current or the resistance.

distractorRationale.a: This is the energy in kWh quoted as a cost, with the tariff omitted
distractorRationale.b: This uses 1.0 × 3.0 = 3 kWh for one day only, then 3 × 50, forgetting the 5 days
distractorRationale.d: This treats 1000 W as 10 kW, or multiplies by an extra factor of 10

questions.stem: Two heating coils P and Q, of resistances 2.0 Ω and 8.0 Ω, are designed to operate from the same 12 V supply. The ratio of the power dissipated in P to that dissipated in Q is
questions.explanation: Both coils see the same voltage, so $P = V^{2}/R$ and power is inversely proportional to resistance. $P_P / P_Q = R_Q / R_P = 8.0 / 2.0 = 4 / 1$. Directly: $P_P = 12^{2}/2.0 = 72\ \text{W}$ and $P_Q = 12^{2}/8.0 = 18\ \text{W}$, so the ratio is 72 : 18 = 4 : 1. Using $I^{2}R$ with the same current would be wrong, because the coils are not in series.

distractorRationale.a: This is R_P : R_Q, which would be the power ratio if the coils carried the same current (series), not the same voltage
distractorRationale.c: This is a square-root mix-up, or the ratio of the resistances reduced by a factor of 2
distractorRationale.d: This is the ratio of the resistances with 8/2 inverted incorrectly to 2 : 1 instead of 4 : 1
